title: How much does a website cost in 2026? What really drives the price

content.imageAlt: Person working on a website on a laptop
content.excerpt: From a few hundred to tens of thousands: why quotes vary so much and what a well-built website should always include.
content.lead: “How much does a website cost?” is the question I get asked most, and the honest answer is: **it depends**. But that’s not a cop-out. In this guide I’ll explain what the price really depends on, why two quotes can be miles apart and what should never be left out.
content.text:
## Why quotes vary so much

You can get offers ranging from a few hundred to tens of thousands of euros, pounds or dollars for what looks like the same job. The difference is rarely the “number of pages”: it’s **what’s included** in the price. Copy written for you or supplied by you, custom design or an off-the-shelf theme, SEO and speed taken care of or ignored, training and support included or extra.

So when you compare two quotes, don’t just look at the total: look at what each one covers.

## What really drives the price

- **Type of website**: a brochure website costs less than an online store or a members’ area.
- **Features**: bookings, configurators, integrations with business software, multiple languages.
- **Content**: whether the copy is written by the professional or supplied by you.
- **Design**: custom-made or adapted from a template.
- **Technical quality**: speed, accessibility, SEO, security.

## What should never be missing

Whatever the budget, a well-built website should include:

- a design that works **on smartphones first**;
- the **SEO** basics: titles, descriptions, structure, structured data;
- good loading **speed**;
- **tracking** of visits and leads, with compliant cookie consent;
- privacy and cookie policies, and compliance with **accessibility** rules where they apply;
- **ownership** of the domain, logins and content in your name.

## Running costs to budget for

On top of the project there are some yearly costs: domain, hosting, any plugin or service licenses, and maintenance (updates, backups, security). Always ask for them to be listed in the quote, so there are no surprises after launch.

## Fixed price or hourly?

With hourly pricing you know what an hour costs, but not what the project will cost. With a **fixed price** you know the final figure from day one, against a clear list of what’s included. For a business that needs to plan a budget, the second is almost always less stressful.

> A good quote isn’t the cheapest one: it’s the one where you understand exactly what you’re buying.

## Where you can save (and where you can’t)

You can save by starting with fewer, well-made pages, supplying ready-made photos and materials, and putting off non-essential features. What you shouldn’t skimp on is speed, SEO and security: they’re what make the website work and, if neglected, cost far more to fix later.

## Questions to ask before you sign

1. What exactly is included, and what isn’t?
2. Who writes the copy?
3. Will the website be mine, with all the logins?
4. How fast will it be, and how will we check?
5. What are the yearly costs after launch?
6. What happens if changes are needed after delivery?
